messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adwoa is a 68-year-old woman who came to the United States from Ghana decades ago, and she now lives with her husband of forty years in a quiet suburban home. The trauma that reshaped her life occurred during her first marriage, a relationship she entered as a young woman in Accra. Her husband then was a charismatic man who, behind closed doors, became someone else entirely. The physical abuse was not constant, but it was unpredictable, and it always followed a pattern: he would accuse her of something—disrespect, imagined infidelity, a meal not prepared to his liking—and then the beating would come. She learned to read the subtle shifts in his voice, the way his jaw tightened, the smell of earth on his hands when he came in from the garden, because that smell often preceded the worst episodes. The memory of those moments is not a story she tells; it is a force that ambushes her. Without any warning, a scent of damp soil from a neighbor's yard will instantly bring back the full sensory weight of that apartment, the feel of the concrete floor against her cheek, the sound of his belt unbuckling. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming, her husband's footsteps on the porch — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore. To stop that force from taking hold, she had learned to keep the television on loud enough that the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy, and noise was her only reliable shield. She finds herself pushing the memory away before she can fully recall it, a reflexive shove that leaves her breathless and disoriented. To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, scrubbing the kitchen counters, reorganizing the pantry, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep.

In the years since, Adwoa has built a life that feels safe on the surface. She remarried a gentle, steady man, and she is grateful for him. But the old patterns have not dissolved; they have simply relocated. She has come to believe that her only reliable safety lies in a very limited number of places: her own living room, the kitchen, the small patch of garden she tends in the back. Everywhere else feels exposed. Even inside her own home, she finds herself on guard, her shoulders tight, her ears tuned to footsteps and the creak of the front door. When her husband travels for a few days, she cannot fall asleep because she needs to stay alert; the bed feels too large, too quiet, and the vulnerability is so acute that she lies rigid, listening. Living at that pitch of constant alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading — a car slowing outside, a neighbor's raised voice, the smell of damp earth from the garden — each one confirming what her body already believed.

To manage this constant low-grade terror, Adwoa has developed a set of strategies that she believes keep her safe. She works hard at keeping busy with other things—scrubbing the kitchen counters, reorganizing the pantry, folding laundry that is already folded. The moment a scent or a thought threatens to pull her back, she turns on the television or calls a friend, keeping her mind occupied all the time. She has also learned to go along with whatever others want, a habit that has deepened over decades. When her church group suggests a potluck at a park, she agrees, even though the smell of cut grass makes her stomach clench. Each place she avoided — the park, the garden club, the grocery store's produce aisle — became a reminder in itself, a daily acknowledgement of what had happened that she could not escape. When a neighbor invites her to a garden club, she accepts, only to cancel at the last minute because the thought of standing among flowerbeds fills her with dread. These small concessions to others feel necessary; she is certain that saying no would draw attention, would make her seem difficult, and being difficult, she has long believed, is dangerous.

The cycle has tightened. The more she distracts herself, the more she avoids the quiet moments when the memories might surface, but the more exhausted she becomes, and exhaustion makes her feel emotionally vulnerable, which in turn triggers the memories again. She has stopped going to the grocery store alone, because the produce section smells of earth after rain, and that smell is a direct line to the past. Her husband has noticed her withdrawing, but she cannot explain it. What finally brought her to seek help was a night last month when he was away, and she found herself standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, clutching a knife, unable to remember why. She is afraid that she is losing her mind. More than anything, she is afraid that if she stops keeping busy, if she lets herself be still, the memory will finish what it started and swallow her whole. And so she kept moving, kept the television on, kept the pantry organized — because the avoidance had grown in all directions until her home was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that the memory itself causes or leads to triggers; instead, triggers lead to the memory, and the memory leads to threat, but the reverse causal direction from memory to triggers is absent.
